rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Islahi says fuller accounts of God’s blessings on David and Solomon appeared in Sūrah Anbiyā’ and Sūrah Naml, so he gives only selected points here.
rows.anchor: Details of the blessings of God on the prophets David (sws) and Solomon (sws) have been mentioned earlier in Sūrah Anbiyā’ and Sūrah Naml.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Tawwīb means adding one’s tune to another’s, repeating another voice, or joining another in chanting.
rows.anchor: The real meaning of بیوأََت is عیترج which is to add one’s tune into another’s, repeat another person’s voice

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The whole universe glorifies God and joins other glorifiers; David’s moving, melodious hymns drew creation into his chanting.
rows.anchor: everything of this universe glorifies the Almighty and when it does so it also joins others who glorify God.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The account of mountains and birds glorifying with David parallels Sūrah Anbiyā’ 21:79.
rows.anchor: In Sūrah Anbiyā’, the words used are:

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The softened iron signifies David’s protective mail armor; the mail was light and wearable while still protecting its wearer.
rows.anchor: The words اَّنَلَأَُو ُهَل َدیِدَحْال portray the weaponry of David viz. the Almighty softened iron for him.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Sābighāt describes loose-fitting attire covering the whole body, here loose-fitting coats of mail.
rows.anchor: The word اتَغِابَس is used for a loose-fitted attire that covers the whole body.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Ṣard means the make or construction of something, while taqdīr means keeping its proportions in view.
rows.anchor: means to keep proportion in consideration while making something.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Making proportioned, loose-fitted iron mail required God to reveal iron-smelting knowledge to David, whose invention advanced defensive weaponry.
rows.anchor: He was the one who originated this technological advancement. With this invention he made a grand contribution to defence weaponry.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The command to do righteous work sets the moral limit for scientific progress: David must not misuse the gift to spread disorder and must remember God watches his deeds.
rows.anchor: the moral right of this advancement is delineated: he should not go astray after being bestowed with this blessing

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The warning applies to David, his family, and followers; Islahi says the Psalms and Proverbs repeat it.
rows.anchor: This directive is given by God to David (sws) and all his family and followers.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Scientific inventions depend on God’s guidance, and every gift or capacity is a trust whose use God observes.
rows.anchor: every invention of science owes itself to God’s guidance. Second, it is the natural requirement of every favour and capability that they be regarded a trust from God

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: When people ignore God’s guidance and their accountability for using gifts, science becomes dangerous; humanity may be destroyed by its own weapons.
rows.anchor: By ignoring both these things, science has become a great danger for man. One cannot say when man may commit suicide from a weapon he has invented himself.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: As David was enabled to use iron, Solomon was enabled to control winds; Islahi links this power to ships making long, unhindered voyages.
rows.anchor: Through this power, Solomon was able to enhance maritime power so much that his ships would travel for months without any hindrance.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Islahi connects Solomon’s wind power with Sūrah Anbiyā’ 21:81, where the stormy wind is made subject to him and directed toward the blessed land.
rows.anchor: for Solomon We subjugated the stormy wind which would blow at his behest to the land in which We placed blessings

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The verse names the wind, the cause, while implying the ships that travel by it; each journey took a month.
rows.anchor: Though winds are mentioned, yet ships are implied. It is as if the cause is mentioned to connote its effect.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Such long voyages imply large ships and a sophisticated, stable system that let them sail in varied seas and wind conditions.
rows.anchor: these ships be of large size and at the same time the system to control the wind be so profound and stable

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Ghuduww and rawāḥ can mean simply coming and going, without specifying morning and evening; he cites Qur’an 3:121 and Aqrab al-mawārid for this usage.
rows.anchor: also occur while being divested of the night and day stipulation to merely mean “coming” and “going.”

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The wind reference highlights Solomon’s naval fleet, just as softened iron earlier highlighted David’s weaponry and military strength; Islahi also points to 21:80.
rows.anchor: It is exactly in line with what was said for David (sws) earlier

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Qiṭr means brass.
rows.anchor: The word ِرْطِق in اَنْلَسَأَُو ُهَل َنْیَع ِرْطِقْال means brass.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Islahi says large brass reserves were discovered in Solomon’s era and used effectively to build and advance society.
rows.anchor: large reserves of brass were discovered and he efficiently used them in the construction and advancement of the society.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Solomon also used brass in the Temple; Islahi compares its fountains in his era with God’s oil fountains today and says discoveries of earthly resources come through divine guidance.
rows.anchor: It is evident from history, that in the construction of the Temple also, Solomon (sws) used this metal.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The insightful recognize God as the source of discoveries, while people dazzled by science wrongly think humans are the source.
rows.anchor: people who have insight know that the real source of all this is God; however, people whose eyes have been dazzled by science think that they are its source.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Solomon’s jinn were not under his independent control; they obeyed him by God’s permission.
rows.anchor: these jinn were not directly under the control of Solomon (sws); in fact, they would obey him on God’s bidding

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The jinn remained accountable to God: any who disobeyed His command would face the torment of Hell.
rows.anchor: he among them who disobeys Our directives, We will make him taste the torment of Hell.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Solomon’s jinn performed construction and other useful tasks for society.
rows.anchor: all related to construction and other needs of the society

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Islahi says Solomon never used the jinn for evil, rebutting occult attributions; he refers to 2:101 for fuller discussion.
rows.anchor: never did he use them for any evil purpose.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: In Islahi’s view, miḥrāb has its ordinary sense of an arch, a prominent feature that first catches an observer’s eye and displays architectural skill.
rows.anchor: The word mih@rāb, in my opinion, is used in its common meaning because arches are the most prominent structure of a building

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Bible’s accounts of Solomon’s Temple and palace construction support Islahi’s description of their elaborate architecture.
rows.anchor: Among the buildings made by Solomon (sws), the details of how the Temple and the palace were constructed are found in the Bible.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Tamāthīl is the plural of timthāl and means an image, carving, portrait, statue, or sculpture; it can depict inanimate things or real and imagined living beings.
rows.anchor: plural of تمثال which refers to the portrait of something or its carved form or its portrait or its statue or sculpture.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Biblical examples include lions, bulls, and cherubim on palace panels, as well as cherubim and floral carvings in the Temple.
rows.anchor: On the panels between the uprights were lions, bulls and cherubim .

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Islahi says there is no disagreement that images and statues of inanimate things are permitted.
rows.anchor: As for the pictures and statues of non-living things, there is no difference of opinion in they being allowed

rows.speaker: our exegetes
rows.claim: Exegetes say living images were permitted under Israelite law, but Islahi rejects this as ignorance of the Torah, which explicitly forbids making images.
rows.anchor: our exegetes that these things were allowed in the sharī‘ah of the Israelites, then this is based on their ignorance from the Torah.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Because the Torah forbids images and Solomon would not violate it, Islahi holds that Solomon’s sculptures depicted art without religious sanctity.
rows.anchor: my opinion is that he would have made only those pictures and statues which related to art alone and did not possess any religious sanctity whatsoever

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Islahi suggests later kings made such images amid Jewish idolatry and attributed them to Solomon to give them religious sanction.
rows.anchor: when idol worship found itself among the Jews, such things must have been made by kings and to give religious sanction to them they must have ascribed them to Solomon (sws).

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: He says Jews also attributed base disciplines to Solomon and portray him in Kings as a materialistic king rather than a prophet, smearing his character.
rows.anchor: the Jews have not presented Solomon (sws) as a prophet of God but as a materialistic king

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Jifān means basins or large plates, while jawāb is the plural of jābiyah and means watering troughs.
rows.anchor: It means basins and large plates and the word ةیجواب is the plural of ةیجاب and means watering-troughs.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Rawāsī is an adjective meaning mountains; here it describes huge, heavy cauldrons fixed in place over a hearth and used to cook large quantities.
rows.anchor: Here it is used for huge cauldrons which would be so heavy that it would not be easy to take them from one place to another.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The passage moves from Solomon’s flourishing arts to his generosity, shown by the great basins and stationary cauldrons made by the jinn.
rows.anchor: The jinn would make huge basins as large as watering-troughs for him and heavy cauldrons which would be stationed at one place.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The phrase “stationary cauldrons” alone conveys great generosity; classical Arab poets use this image for generous people such as Ḥātim al-Ṭāʾī.
rows.anchor: It is this metaphor which classical Arab poets use for their generous people like H@atim al-T@ā’ī

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A blessed civilization combines art and science with generosity toward the needy; artistic grandeur alongside the poor’s suffering is a fiendish society.
rows.anchor: A society in which both these aspects simultaneously exist is a blessed one.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Solomon is told to remain righteous, show gratitude for gifts of science and art, and use every blessing properly; prophets receive this general duty by revelation.
rows.anchor: he should not be led away from the path of righteousness after receiving the gifts of science and art

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The address to the House of David includes Solomon, his family, and followers, who should imitate David’s gratitude; Solomon inherited blessings granted to his grateful father.
rows.anchor: remind Solomon (sws), his family and his followers to follow his father in thanking God.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Few people are grateful after receiving blessings, and the trial of gratitude is harder than the trial of patience.
rows.anchor: this path is not easy to tread; it is fraught with danger.

rows.speaker: Jesus (sws)
rows.claim: Jesus’ comparison of a camel passing through a needle’s eye with a rich person entering God’s kingdom corroborates the difficulty of gratitude.
rows.anchor: it is easier for a camel to go through the eye of a needle than for someone who is rich to enter the kingdom of God.
